https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-r.text: WARSAW — A bad-tempered split in Poland’s right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party is being greeted with joy by the centrist, pro-EU government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, but it’s unclear whether it will improve his odds of retaining power in next year’s election. Tusk’s Civic Coalition is far ahead in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls — with 32 percent support, compared with PiS’s 21 percent — but that does not offer a full picture of the electoral dynamics. All of the parties on the right together could still command a majority — but only if they’re able to cobble together a coalition after next year’s vote. Three of Tusk’s four junior coalition partners may fail to clear the 5 percent threshold needed to enter parliament. Renata Mieńkowska-Norkiene, a political scientist at the University of Warsaw, called Tusk’s chances in the 2027 race “far from certain.” Advertisement Advertisement However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right. PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month , when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies. The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious. Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support. “Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week. He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future. Advertisement Advertisement Kaczyński responded by appearing to question both Morawiecki’s loyalty and his state of mind. “Mateusz Morawiecki’s latest statements show clearly that his enemy is not Tusk, but me and Law and Justice. I have the impression that the prime minister is in some peculiar state. God willing, I am wrong,” Kaczyński said in a post on X. He twisted the knife in another post on Friday , denouncing “attacks based on lies, manipulation, and insinuations,” made by “people who, until recently, pretended they wanted to be part of PiS but decided to break away.” Mateusz Morawiecki is pictured in Brussels in March 2023. | Pool photo by Olivier Matthys via AFP/Getty Images Tusk is watching the fallout with joy. “I watch what is happening with a smile,” Tusk said at a press conference last week when asked about the turmoil within the largest opposition party. Unclear political picture Although PiS and Civic Coalition have been alternating in power for more than two decades, Poland’s current political makeup is a lot more complicated. Advertisement Advertisement Two new parties are battling for votes on the far-right — the libertarian Confederation, with 14 percent support, and the antisemitic extremist Confederation of the Polish Crown, at 11 percent. The two far-right parties are fighting each other, and also taking aim at PiS. “I feel the next prime minister should not be from PiS,” Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, said in a radio interview this week. Wojciech Machulski, a party spokesperson, denounced Morawiecki as a “puppet” with a terrible governing record but also noted : “Kaczyński is no longer the leader of the right; he no longer dominates the right.” Political analysts warned that Tusk should not assume the split will benefit his coalition. The Kaczyński and Morawiecki parties could appeal to a broader range of voters by campaigning separately, while Tusk’s prospects depend heavily on the survival of the weakest members of his coalition, said Mieńkowska-Norkiene. Advertisement Advertisement “What is more, Morawiecki could attract more conservative voters from those parties,” she added. Morawiecki is already campaigning in an effort to reach beyond PiS’s traditional right-wing electorate — this week laying out a new strategy to combat Poland’s low birth rate. “A right-wing party without a clear identity-based agenda will not be a right-wing party. But a right-wing party without a development agenda and without the ability to implement change will never come to power,” he said in his party manifesto . Anna Siewierska-Chmaj, a political scientist at the University of Rzeszów, said Tusk’s governing coalition should not rely on its enemies devouring themselves and should instead use the summer break to overhaul its political messaging. Many voters are fed up with the government’s lackluster results — although part of that stems from PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki blocking a lot of legislation. “The old polarization strategy of ‘us versus PiS’ will no longer suffice,” she said.

Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPA View image in fullscreen Mahmoud Khalil outside Columbia University in New York, New York, on 14 September 2026. Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPA Mahmoud Khalil Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia University over years of alleged anti-Palestinian discrimination Lawsuit accuses university of ‘deliberate indifference’ and failure to respond to ‘persistent and coordinated harassment’ Alice Speri Mon 14 Sep 2026 20.34 BST Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.20 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mahmoud Khalil announced on Monday that he’s sued Columbia University , accusing the New York City school he attended of a years-long history of anti-Palestinian discrimination, indifference to harassment, and retaliation. Khalil, a US green card holder of Palestinian descent, was a graduate student at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs (SIPA) when he was arrested at his university apartment by federal immigration agents in March 2025, the first of a number of foreign nationals that the Trump administration has detained and sought to deport over their pro-Palestinian advocacy. In a 60-page complaint filed in the southern district of New York , Khalil and members of the SIPA’s Palestine Working Group have now accused the university, its board, and the dean of the school, Keren Yarhi-Milo, of “deliberate indifference” and failure to respond to “severe, persistent, and coordinated harassment” directed towards him and other students who had been outspoken about Palestinian rights. Khalil, who missed the birth of his first son while in detention, was released in June 2025 but is continuing to fight the administration’s efforts to deport him – a protracted legal battle that is expected to ultimately be decided by the US supreme court . Still, Khalil has continued to speak out, both about Palestinian rights and about free speech in the US. In July, he sued the Trump administration and several pro-Israel groups, accusing them of conspiring to target him and others as punishment for their advocacy. Separately, he has filed a $20m false imprisonment and malicious prosecution case against the administration and sued them for records of collusion with anti-Palestinian doxxing groups including Canary Mission. In an earlier lawsuit filed in March 2025 he also sought to stop Columbia from releasing student disciplinary records to the House committee on education and the workforce, which has led the charge against universities in the aftermath of Israel’s war in Gaza and widespread campus protests in support of Palestinian rights. “Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration through its deliberate indifference and discrimination aimed at intimidating Palestinian students,” Khalil wrote in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “For over two years, we pleaded with Columbia. Columbia did not care. Our safety and our wellbeing did not serve the ideological project its Board of Trustees was protecting, so they traded us away.” Khalil also warned of more lawsuits to come. “Next, I will turn to the hateful individuals at Columbia who were also responsible for what we endured,” he wrote. A spokesperson for the university declined to comment on pending litigation but said that “Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise.” Columbia students were the first to erect pro-Palestinian encampments on campus in the spring of 2024, inspiring dozens more across the country. The university, once home to cutting-edge scholarship about Palestine, also became the first to be targeted by the Trump administration as part of its ongoing effort to exploit antisemitism accusations to bend universities to its agenda. As tensions flared on campus after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, students repeatedly sought the administration’s support to protect them from doxing campaigns, the complaint alleges. Many had their photos, names, and personal information posted online, as well as on mobile billboard trucks. Mohammed Ibrahim Zubairi, a Columbia graduate and former president of the Palestine Working Group who is also a named plaintiff in the lawsuit, told the Guardian that the litigation is an effort to “force a reckoning within these institutions, so that they may recognize they have ended up on the wrong side of history”. “For me, this case is about the environment in which the hostility that I and other pro-Palestinian students experienced was able to persist,” echoed Bhavana Bellamkonda, another plaintiff. Mahmoud Khalil sues Trump officials and pro-Israel groups over ‘conspiracy’ to target him Read more “What we are asking for is not special treatment,” she told the Guardian. “We are asking for the same protections that Columbia students are entitled to under state and federal law, and that Columbia itself has represented that it provides to its tuition-paying students.” Khalil was well known to university administrators because of his efforts to mediate between student protesters and school officials. In the months leading up to his detention, he reported threats, harassment, and doxing, including attacks targeting his immigration status. On 7 March 2025, a day before his arrest, he emailed Columbia’s then interim president, Katrina Armstrong, and other administrators, urging them to take immediate action to protect international students. “What Mahmoud Khalil endured for speaking up against the genocide in Gaza was unconscionable. And much of that was at the hands of or enabled by Columbia,” Brittany Finley, one of his attorneys, wrote in a press release. “Columbia knew what was happening on its campus, and it chose indifference over action.” According to the complaint, rather than address Khalil’s and other students’ concerns, Columbia subjected students to disciplinary proceedings and restrictions, including suspending SIPA’s Palestine Working Group in May 2025 – a suspension that remains in effect. Other pro-Palestinians students have also sued Columbia over its alleged failure to protect them from a hostile campus environment. “This didn’t begin with me, nor does it end with me,” Khalil said. “With this lawsuit, we hope to ensure that future generations of Columbia students never have to face this fight.” Explore more on these topics Mahmoud Khalil Columbia University US universities Israel-Gaza war New York US immigration Trump administration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.bursa.ro/security-forum-nato.text: NATO is ready to fight at any moment to defend Europe, and any adversary attempting to occupy the territory of an allied state must know that it will encounter a force capable of blocking its attack, halting its advance and, if the aggression continues, destroying the military system it has committed to the fight, General Alexus Gregory Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said yesterday at the Warsaw Security Forum, which is taking place over two days in the Polish capital. At the heart of his address was what the general calls the "theory of victory”: a shared vision of how NATO deters an attack and defends the territory of its 32 allies if deterrence fails. "If we are attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent. We will continue to prepare and train every day, and we will be more ready tomorrow and even more ready the day after tomorrow. Our combat readiness under this theory of victory means, first and foremost, winning in defence. Demonstrating our readiness is also central to preventing conflict,” Alexus Grynkewich stated. NATO's military chief in Europe explained that this concept is based on the strategy for deterrence and defence of the Euro-Atlantic area, agreed upon by all allies. According to him, it is not a military plan in the strict sense of the term, but rather the framework that tells NATO forces what they must be able to do and what capabilities they must demonstrate to convince an adversary that aggression will fail. General Alexus Grynkewich explained: "We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent the enemy's advance. And, if necessary, we will destroy the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system deployed against us.” These three stages-"block, blunt, break”-describe the progression from stopping the assault to preventing the offensive from continuing and, ultimately, destroying the mechanism that sustains it. Blunting the attack means reducing the adversary's ability to advance and seize the initiative. Grynkewich is not promising a war without losses, but explaining how NATO intends to prevent the occupation and retention of allied territory. "To block, our land forces will manoeuvre to dominate any enemy assault at the point of contact. Through manoeuvre, we will fix enemy formations and prevent the occupation of Alliance territory. Land forces will attack the enemy and destroy its advancing forces. But they will not do this alone: our air and naval forces, working together with our space and cyber forces, will rapidly gain freedom of manoeuvre, quickly securing air and maritime superiority in and above the battlespace,” the Supreme Allied Commander Europe explained. If the attacker continues, the response will also target its forces' supply, command and support capabilities. NATO intends to combine high-tech precision weaponry with large numbers of affordable systems that can be produced at scale, simultaneously employing land, air, maritime, space and cyber assets. "Should the adversary choose to continue the attack or commit its reserves, we will destroy the warfighting system committed against us. This includes not only the attacking force itself, but everything that supports, sustains or controls that force,” Alexus Grynkewich said, adding: "Enemy formations will be deprived of supplies, enemy commanders will no longer be able to control their forces, and enemy support capabilities and forces will be degraded and destroyed.” *NATO's Eastern Flank plays a priority role in the military alliance's new strategy NATO's Eastern Flank holds an essential place in this concept. The Supreme Allied Commander described the military forces in the region as ready to respond now, while training and investment continue to strengthen their defensive capabilities. Forward-deployed units on the Eastern Flank must demonstrate that they can block an attack, while air and maritime forces must demonstrate that they can support efforts to halt it. "Our forward-deployed land forces on the Eastern Flank will train and demonstrate their ability to block any attack. Our air and maritime forces will train and demonstrate their ability to gain and maintain freedom of manoeuvre and deliver multidomain effects to further blunt any attack,” Alexus Grynkewich stated, announcing investments in long-range precision strikes, affordable systems, sensor networks and a "combat cloud”. Regarding ammunition stockpiles, the commander expressed confidence in the available resources, but stressed the need to be able to sustain a prolonged conflict: "We need not only the initial capability, but also the ability to sustain it over the long term. I am looking very closely at stockpiles across the Alliance, I am very reassured about what we have available today, and I know we will continue to improve them.” However, General Alexus Grynkewich firmly defined the purpose of these preparations and reiterated that NATO seeks to stop aggression and defend its territory, while the stated military objective is to defeat the forces attacking the Alliance. "We are not seeking to inflict a strategic defeat on our adversary, nor do we need to do so. On the contrary, we seek only to stop any attack in its tracks to deny the ability to occupy and hold our territory. Achieving this objective requires the tactical and operational defeat of the forces used against us, but nothing more,” General Grynkewich explained, adding: "I am not saying that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It is not.” But he pointed out that combat readiness remains necessary, because planning must consider "what is possible, not just what is probable”. Asked about the strength of the political commitment to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty, concerning collective defence, Grynkewich said he trusted the promises made by allied leaders. The Supreme Allied Commander Europe noted that the declaration adopted at the NATO summit in Ankara expresses an unequivocal shared commitment: "All 32 allies signed an extremely strong declaration that speaks of an unwavering commitment to Article 5, and I take our heads of state and government at their word.” Alexus Grynkewich cited the American military presence on the Eastern Flank as evidence of NATO commitments being honoured. "We have American troops here in Poland today. We have American troops deployed across the entire eastern flank. Ultimately, it is a political decision as to who provides troops and where, but I believe no one should question the United States' commitment to this Alliance,” the Supreme Allied Commander stated. In the face of sabotage and other hybrid attacks attributed to Russia, Grynkewich called for coordination among allies, public attribution of responsibility when legal requirements are met, and a response that would counter Moscow's objective of weakening Western support for Ukraine. Increasing military assistance to Kyiv would convey, he explained, that such actions strengthen the allies' resolve. His speech ended with a warning intended to reach both the populations of NATO states and potential aggressors: "Our Alliance exists to preserve peace. But let there be no doubt: if war comes, we will block, we will blunt any attack and then, if it does not stop, we will destroy the forces carrying out aggression against us.” *Zelenskyy: "Putin does not read Truth Social” Alexus Grynkewich's military message complemented the political warnings delivered at the opening of the forum by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius. Their remarks linked Europe's security to Ukraine's resistance and Europeans' ability to strengthen their defence. In the Polish prime minister's assessment, Moscow's ambitions extend beyond Ukraine's borders. "Russia wants to dominate Ukraine, and we know it will not stop pursuing its plans. Russia wants to destroy the existing security architecture in Europe to ensure that Russian domination returns to where it was before 1989. We have no doubt about this,” Donald Tusk said, calling on the West to respond with a stronger deterrence policy, particularly through sanctions. He cited attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as evidence of the gap between diplomatic initiatives and Russia's behaviour: "It is the same every time: if you propose that Russia stop striking critical infrastructure or civilian facilities, the response is brutal and arrogant. We can no longer harbour any illusions: Russia is not interested in de-escalation, a ceasefire or peace, but only in domination.” Volodymyr Zelenskyy described this gap through the actual situation in Ukrainian cities. According to the Ukrainian president, Donald Trump's announcement of an energy truce was accompanied by new Russian attacks, while emergency crews were trying to restore electricity and water supplies. "Yesterday, we were all surprised when, following an unexpected but very important post by the American president saying that he had secured an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, at that very moment Russian jet-powered drones were flying through our skies, and large parts of Kyiv had no water or electricity,” Zelenskyy said. He added: "It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social, and his Shahed drones follow a different set of instructions.” The Ukrainian president stated that his country accepts a mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. The condition is that Russia must honour the same obligation, at a time when electricity and the functioning of the networks are vital to the population. "If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its refineries and its oil exports, then Russia must stop striking our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people. This is fair,” Zelenskyy stated. Kyiv's offer, he insisted, is explicit: "We are ready to honour an energy truce if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree too, and we have already shown that we are serious.” *Presidential elections in Ukraine only after a complete ceasefire lasting at least 60 days Zelenskyy called for American pressure on Moscow and continued European support, ranging from ammunition for F-16 aircraft and air-defence interceptors to funding for Ukrainian weapons and drone production. "We need American pressure on Russia-not an easing of sanctions, not concessions, but real pressure,” he stated. The president also warned about hybrid operations directed against Europe: "Please do not underestimate the threats to your own countries. There is no such thing as a small act of destabilisation. Our intelligence services know that Russia is planning many, many aggressive hybrid operations against Europe, against various countries, against your countries.” Regarding elections in Ukraine, Zelenskyy linked the possibility of holding them to a complete ceasefire. He cited the ongoing attacks and the difficulty of enabling soldiers on the front line to vote, declaring himself willing to seek legislative solutions together with parliament. "And if we have a complete ceasefire lasting at least 60 days, then I will be ready to work towards holding elections,” the Ukrainian president explained. Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space, raised the issue of Europe's ability to translate these warnings into resources, industrial production and joint decisions. The European Commission official argued that greater responsibility for conventional defence is needed, given that China's rise will direct American resources towards Asia. "Strengthening defence capabilities is an exclusively European responsibility, not because the United States is no longer a partner, but because of global geopolitical developments: China's rise will lead to the reorientation of American resources towards that region. Europe must assume primary responsibility for conventional defence under the NATO 3.0 concept, reducing its dependence on American strategic enablers and strengthening NATO's European pillar,” Andrius Kubilius stated. He explained that defence remains primarily the responsibility of the member states, in coordination with NATO, while the European Union can mobilise economic instruments to finance joint projects. The main obstacle identified by the commissioner is the fragmentation of Europe's defence industry and the lack of an integrated market. In this context, Kubilius mentioned consideration of the possibility of creating a European Security Council that would include the EU states, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and even Canada. "American military experts are sending a clear message about the need for Europe to become stronger, and this requires greater political unity. A major problem is the fragmentation of the defence industry (...) and the lack of an integrated market. The creation of the Security Council would provide member states with the framework needed to make practical decisions and overcome this fragmentation,” the European commissioner said. The first day of the Warsaw Security Forum also included discussions on combating cyberattacks, building new energy capacity to serve defence industry factories and ensure energy security along the north-south axis, and establishing a joint military force to ensure the EU's security. As this edition went to press, a debate was underway on the impact that the outcome of the US midterm elections would have on NATO. Discussions continue today, when participants will address the new European security architecture, the EU enlargement process, peace negotiations in the Middle East, and how Russia and China want to shape the new world order. Articol despre NATO, Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander, Donald Tusk, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Andrius Kubilius.
